sections.heading: What are the main types of seizure and what do they feel like?
sections.body:
Epilepsy seizures are grouped by where they start in the brain and how much of it is involved. Focal seizures start in one area on one side of the brain, and some people stay aware during them while for others awareness is affected. Generalised seizures involve both sides of the brain from the start, and a person does not usually stay conscious during them.

Some people notice a warning before a seizure, called an aura. An aura is usually a focal seizure in its own right. Examples include a strange feeling that is hard to describe, a rising feeling in the tummy, a feeling that events have happened before, unusual smells or tastes, and tingling in the arms and legs.

In a tonic-clonic seizure the person loses consciousness and the muscles go stiff, so someone who is standing may fall. This is followed by repeated jerking of the arms or legs. A seizure that begins on one side of the brain can also spread to both sides, which is called a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

sections.heading: How is epilepsy diagnosed?
sections.body:
Epilepsy Action advises seeing a GP as soon as possible after a suspected seizure, even if you did not go to hospital at the time. For a first suspected seizure, children over 2, young adults and adults should see an epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks of the GP making the referral. The GP may arrange some tests while you wait to see the specialist.

No single test can confirm epilepsy. An EEG may be requested, and if it is done after a first seizure it should be done as soon as possible. A normal EEG does not rule epilepsy out, although a positive finding can support a provisional diagnosis. NICE recommends an MRI scan for most people who are diagnosed with epilepsy. An MRI scan cannot decide on its own whether someone has epilepsy, but together with other information it can help the clinician judge whether epilepsy is a likely cause.

Epilepsy Action advises keeping a seizure diary and taking it to the appointment. If the diagnosis stays unclear, further investigations or referral to a specialist epilepsy centre should be considered.

sections.heading: How is epilepsy treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says anti-seizure medicines are the most commonly used treatment for epilepsy. They help control seizures in around 7 out of 10 people. They do not cure epilepsy, but they can stop seizures happening. Some anti-seizure medicines can make some types of contraception, including the combined pill and implants, less effective, so this is worth raising with a doctor or nurse.

Other options are considered when medicines do not control the seizures. Only a minority of people with hard-to-control epilepsy are candidates for traditional epilepsy surgery. Vagus nerve stimulation is another non-drug option that is used for epilepsy that has not responded to medicines. The NHS says a ketogenic diet is sometimes recommended for children whose seizures are not controlled by medicines. It should only be used under the supervision of an epilepsy specialist with the help of a dietitian.

sections.heading: What should happen if someone has a seizure?
sections.body:
NHS advice for a convulsive seizure is to support the person gently, cushion their head and not try to move them. The NHS also advises not putting anything in their mouth and not restraining them unless they are in immediate danger. Once the convulsions stop, the advice is to place the person in the recovery position, stay with them and note when the seizure started and finished.

The NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance if it is the person's first seizure, if the seizure lasts longer than is usual for them, or if it lasts more than 5 minutes and their usual pattern is not known. A 999 call is also advised if the person does not regain full consciousness, has several seizures without regaining consciousness, is seriously injured or has trouble breathing afterwards. NHS inform describes status epilepticus, a seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery in between, as a medical emergency.

sections.heading: Living with epilepsy and the outlook
sections.body:
The NHS suggests keeping a diary to spot triggers such as tiredness, stress, a period, flashing lights, food or drink. Epilepsy Action says that too little sleep or missing epilepsy medicines can lead to more seizures. Some people find that stress-relieving activities such as exercise, yoga and meditation help.

In the UK, the NHS says that a person must stop driving after any type of seizure and tell the DVLA. When driving can start again depends on the type of seizure and when it last happened. Epilepsy can also mean thinking carefully about certain jobs, swimming, contraception and planning a pregnancy.

For most people, an epileptic seizure usually stops by itself and does not cause any lasting problems. The main risks are injury, seizures that go on for a long time and, rarely, sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. The NHS describes this sudden death as rare, and says epilepsy treatment can reduce the risk. The risk appears to be higher with frequent or poorly controlled seizures, which is why seizure control matters. Anti-suffocation pillows have no research evidence that they reduce the risk.

faqs.a: The NHS says anti-seizure medicines do not cure epilepsy, but they can stop seizures happening. They help control seizures in around 7 out of 10 people. When medicines do not work well enough, other options such as surgery, nerve stimulation or a special diet may be discussed with an epilepsy specialist.

faqs.q: Does a normal EEG mean it is not epilepsy?
faqs.a: No. A normal routine EEG does not rule epilepsy out. A positive result can support a provisional diagnosis, but no single test can confirm epilepsy. Doctors weigh the EEG together with the story of what happened, any scan results and other information.

faqs.q: Can I drive after a seizure?
faqs.a: In the UK, the NHS says a person must stop driving after any type of seizure and tell the DVLA. When they can start again depends on the type of seizure and when it last happened. This applies to the UK, and the rules differ in other countries, so anyone living elsewhere should check their local rules.

An aura is a warning feeling that often comes before a seizure. It is usually a focal seizure in its own right. People describe a hard-to-describe strange feeling, a rising feeling in the tummy, a feeling that events have happened before, unusual smells or tastes, or tingling in the arms and legs.

faqs.q: When should I call 999 for a seizure?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 if it is the person's first seizure, if the seizure lasts longer than usual for them, or if it lasts more than 5 minutes and their usual pattern is not known. It also advises calling if the person does not regain full consciousness, has several seizures without recovering in between, is seriously injured or has trouble breathing afterwards.
